feedback: If a learner drops the spider into INSECT, have them re-count its legs one at a time: marking or lighting legs 1 through 8 and splitting the body into 2 parts shows 'arachnid, not an insect'.
When a sort is justified by 'it's small' or 'it lives in the garden', redirect: 'Two things can both be small — only the leg count and body parts decide. What did you count?'
If a learner insists a spider has 6 legs to make it fit, count the legs together by touching each one; separate 'what I want it to be' from 'what I actually counted' — 8 legs means not an insect.
Confirm correct feature-based reasoning: '6 legs and 3 parts, so insect — yes, that's exactly how classification works.'
activities.intendedInsight: Classification means grouping by a definite, countable feature, not by appearance. An insect is defined by 6 legs and 3 body parts; creatures that fail this test (spider 8 legs/2 parts, woodlouse 14 legs, worm no legs, snail no legs/shell+foot) belong to other groups.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of real minibeast photos (e.g. ant, beetle, spider, woodlouse, worm, snail) and two bins labelled INSECT and NOT AN INSECT.
Before placing each creature, count its legs and its body parts — touching or marking each leg as you count so you don't miss any.
Place the creature in a bin and say the reason aloud in the form: 'It has ___ legs and ___ body parts, so it is / is not an insect.'
Check the spider carefully: count all 8 legs and notice its body is in 2 parts; place it in NOT AN INSECT and name it an arachnid.

Check the woodlouse (14 legs) and the worm (no legs) the same way. Handle the snail as a clear non-insect 'other': it has no legs (a shell and one muscular foot), so it fails the six-legs test — do not try to fit it to a leg-count group. Confirm the beetle and ant have 6 legs and 3 parts and belong in INSECT.
Expert round: re-sort into four bins — insect / arachnid / crustacean / other — and justify each placement by its distinguishing feature.
activities.title: Is it an insect? Sort-and-count

feedback: If the learner accepts 'spiders are bugs so they're insects', return to the count: 8 legs is the single feature that decides it.

For the caterpillar prompt, clarify that a caterpillar is the larval life stage of an insect (it becomes a butterfly or moth) — being an insect or not is about the group, not how it looks at one stage.
activities.intendedInsight: Surfacing the misconception in role makes the learner defend or reject 'insect' with the counted feature rather than with a feeling about what counts as a 'bug'.
learnerActions: Act out or read a short exchange in which a spider objects: 'I'm NOT an insect — count my legs!'
Respond by actually counting the spider's legs (8) and body parts (2) and stating the group it belongs to.

Discuss a stage-vs-group counterexample: a caterpillar looks worm-like but is the young stage of an insect that becomes a butterfly or moth. Treat this as a discussion of life stage versus group only — not as a leg-counting case, since a caterpillar's prolegs can make a raw leg count misleading.
Discuss: could something be tiny and live in the garden and STILL not be an insect? Give an example (spider, worm, woodlouse, snail).
activities.title: The spider sets the record straight

feedback: Full grasp: sorts all four correctly, rejects the spider with '8 legs / 2 body parts', and explains differences (worm = no legs, woodlouse = 14) rather than reciting one fact.
Partial grasp: states the six-legs rule but applies it unevenly — e.g. rejects the worm but slips the spider or woodlouse in; prompt them to count again and give the feature reason each time.
Gap: puts spider/worm/woodlouse in the insect box and sorts by size or creepiness — re-establish counting legs as the sole gate before sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the deciding feature for each creature distinguishes a learner who owns the six-legs/three-parts rule from one relying on 'it's small and creepy'.
learnerActions: Someone put a spider in the 'insect' box — decide whether that is right.
Sort these four — spider, ant, woodlouse, worm — into 'insect' and 'not insect'.
For each one, say HOW you decided (which feature you counted).
Answer the follow-ups: give the one feature that proves the spider is out; say whether a 14-legged woodlouse is an insect and which rule tells you.
activities.title: Explain-your-decision check
